The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $V$ be a Banach space and let $W\subseteq V$ be a closed linear subspace,
equipped with the restricted norm. Then $W$ is a Banach space.

derivations.claim: Define $\ell(q):=\int_Dq\,dx$. By [F2], $|\ell(q)|\le |D|^{1/2}\|q\|_2$, and linearity of the integral makes $\ell$ a bounded real linear functional. Its kernel is exactly $L^2_0(D)$.

The kernel of a continuous functional is closed: if $q_n\in L^2_0(D)$ and $q_n\to q$ in $L^2$, then $|\ell(q)|=|\ell(q-q_n)|\le |D|^{1/2}\|q-q_n\|_2\to0$, so $\ell(q)=0$. Thus $L^2_0(D)$ is a closed linear subspace of $L^2(D)$.

The inner product on $L^2(D)$ restricts to an inner product on $L^2_0(D)$ and induces the inherited $L^2$ norm. By [F1], $L^2(D)$ is complete; by [F3] and step 2.1, its closed subspace $L^2_0(D)$ is complete. Therefore it is a real Hilbert space with the restricted inner product.

$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from

locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

derivations.claim: Choose $c\in K$ and $s\in(0,1)$, and put $T_s(x)=c+s(x-c)$ and $U_s=T_s^{-1}(K)$. Since $K$ is convex and $c$ is interior, $T_s(\overline K)$ is a compact subset of $K$; hence $U_s$ is an open simplex containing $\overline K$ with positive distance from $\overline K$ to $U_s^c$. Define $u_s=u\circ T_s$ on $U_s$. For $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U_s)$, change variables $y=T_s(x)$ in the weak derivative identity of $u$; with $\widetilde\psi(y)=\psi(T_s^{-1}y)$ one has $D_{y_i}\widetilde\psi=s^{-1}(D_{x_i}\psi)\circ T_s^{-1}$, so the identity gives $D_i u_s=s(D_i u)\circ T_s$ distributionally.

For any $g\in L^2(K)$, extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^d$. Given $\eta>0$, choose $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ with $\|g-\phi\|_{L^2(K)}<\eta$ by [F2]. Because $T_s(K)\subset K$, change of variables [F3] gives $\|(g-\phi)\circ T_s\|_{L^2(K)}\le s^{-d/2}\eta$, while uniform continuity of $\phi$ on $\overline K$ gives $\|\phi\circ T_s-\phi\|_{L^2(K)}\to0$ as $s\to1^-$. The triangle inequality and arbitrary $\eta$ therefore show $\|g\circ T_s-g\|_{L^2(K)}\to0$.
Apply step 1.2 to $g=u$ and to every $g=D_i u$. By step 1.1, $D_i u_s=s(D_i u)\circ T_s$, and $s\to1$; hence $u_s|_K\to u$ in the full $H^1(K)$ norm as $s\to1^-$.

Each zero extension is in $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$; [F5] therefore gives $\|w_\delta-u_s\|_{H^1(K)}\to0$ as $\delta\to0^+$. Choose $\delta<r$ small enough to make this norm less than $\varepsilon/2$. Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$

almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev

is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded, connected polyhedral Lipschitz domain. A matching affine simplicial mesh and its shape regularity have the exact meaning of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; additionally, call the mesh facet-connected when its dual graph (one vertex per cell and one edge per shared $(d-1)$-facet) is connected. Write $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$.

For $k\ge0$, $\mathbb P_k(K)$ is the real scalar polynomial space of total degree at most $k$, and $\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k$ is the real homogeneous scalar polynomial space of degree exactly $k$ (for $k=0$, the constants). Define
$$\operatorname{RT}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)+x\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k(K),\qquad \operatorname{BDM}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)\quad(k\ge1).$$
For either local family $X_k$, its global H(div)-conforming space is
$$X_k(\mathcal T_h)=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):v|_K\in X_k(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.
$$
The zero-normal RT0 flux space and mean-zero P0 pressure space are
$$V_h:=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D),\qquad Q_h:=\{q\in L^2(D):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K,\ \int_Dq=0\}.$$
For each mesh facet $F$, fix one unit normal $n_F$; on a cell boundary use the outward unit normal $n_K$, which equals either $n_F$ or $-n_F$. The notation $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ means cellwise constants. No existence of a mesh for every $D$ is asserted by this definition.

Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an orientation-preserving affine bijection between nondegenerate $d$-simplices, with $J=\det A>0$, and use the contravariant Piola map of [[def-na-contravariant-piola-map]]. For every $k\ge0$, it maps $\operatorname{RT}_k(\widehat K)$ bijectively onto $\operatorname{RT}_k(K)$, and for every $k\ge1$ it maps $\operatorname{BDM}_k(\widehat K)$ bijectively onto $\operatorname{BDM}_k(K)$.

Let $F_K(\widehat x)=A_K\widehat x+b_K$ be as in [[def-na-contravariant-piola-map]], and let $\widehat v\in C^1(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb R^d)$. Set $v=\mathcal P_K\widehat v$. Then
$$
(\operatorname{div}_x v)(F_K(\widehat x))=J_K^{-1}\operatorname{div}_{\widehat x}\widehat v(\widehat x).
$$
For each facet $\widehat F$ mapped to $F$, with the corresponding oriented normals, the integrated flux is preserved:
$$
\int_F v\cdot n_F\,ds=\int_{\widehat F}\widehat v\cdot\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat s.
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Assume Countable Choice. For a nondegenerate affine simplex $K$ with diameter $h_K$ and shape bound $h_K/r_K\le\gamma$, and any facet $F$, every $u\in H^1(K)$ has a well-defined trace $\gamma_Fu\in L^2(F)$ and
$$
\|\gamma_Fu\|_{L^2(F)}^2\le C(d,\gamma)\bigl(h_K^{-1}\|u\|_{L^2(K)}^2+h_K\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(K)}^2\bigr).
$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a polyhedral open set with a conforming affine simplicial mesh, let $K_+$ and $K_-$ share an interior facet $F$, and let $w\in H^1(D)$. The elementwise $L^2(F)$ traces of $w|_{K_+}$ and $w|_{K_-}$ agree almost everywhere on $F$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nondegenerate open simplex. For every $u\in H^1(K;\mathbb R)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a function $u_\varepsilon$ smooth on an open neighborhood of $\overline K$ with $\|u_\varepsilon-u\|_{H^1(K)}<\varepsilon$.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev-space interfaces below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and $v\in H(\operatorname{div};D)$. Define the trace quotient
$$T_D:=H^1(D)/H^1_0(D),\qquad \|[w]\|_{T_D}:=\inf_{z\in H^1_0(D)}\|w+z\|_{H^1(D)}.$$
Then the formula
$$
\langle\gamma_n v,[w]\rangle:=\int_D\bigl(v\cdot\nabla w+(\operatorname{div}v)w\bigr)\,dx
$$
is independent of the representative $w$, defines a bounded real linear functional $\gamma_n v\in T_D'$, and satisfies $\|\gamma_n v\|_{T_D'}\le\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}$. This functional is the weak normal trace; no pointwise boundary value is asserted.

For an open set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, let $T_D=H^1(D)/H^1_0(D)$ be the trace quotient of [[lem-na-hdiv-weak-normal-trace]], and let $\gamma_n:H(\operatorname{div};D)\to T_D'$ be its weak normal trace. Define
$$
H_0(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):\gamma_n v=0\text{ in }T_D'\}.
$$
Thus zero normal trace means that the Green-duality functional vanishes on every H1 trace class; no pointwise normal value is required.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

derivations.claim: On the reference simplex $\widehat S_d=\{x_i>0,\sum_i x_i<1\}$, each coordinate facet has outward normal $-e_i$ and area $1/(d-1)!$, while the top facet has outward normal $(1,\ldots,1)/\sqrt d$ and area $\sqrt d/(d-1)!$. For $\widehat v=a+cx$, the constant-vector facet fluxes sum to zero by [F3], and the flux sum of $cx$ is $c/(d-1)!=dc|\widehat S_d|$. If all facet fluxes vanish then $c=0$; the coordinate-facet fluxes then force each $a_i=0$. The flux map is injective between spaces of dimension $d+1$, hence bijective.

For any physical simplex, [F2] transports the reference flux degrees of freedom bijectively, so the same unisolvence holds. On each facet, $(a+cx)\cdot n$ is constant because $x\cdot n$ is constant on its supporting hyperplane; equal integrated fluxes therefore give equal normal components.

Let $v$ be a piecewise RT0 field with matching shared-facet fluxes. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, apply [F3] to $\phi v$ cellwise and sum: interior facet terms cancel by step 2.1 and the common value of $\phi$, and boundary terms vanish because $\phi$ is compactly supported. Thus $\int_Dv\cdot\nabla\phi=-\sum_K\int_K(\operatorname{div}v)\phi$. The cellwise divergence is constant and in $L^2$, so $v\in H(\operatorname{div};D)$ by definition.

Conversely, let $v$ be a piecewise RT0 field in H(div), with global $L^2$ divergence $g$. For every test supported in one cell, the global distributional identity and cellwise Gauss–Green give zero pairing with $g$ minus that cell's polynomial divergence. This difference is in $L^2(K)$ and hence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(K)$ by [F7]; extending from real to complex tests by linearity, injectivity [F7] makes the difference zero almost everywhere on the cell. For arbitrary $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, summing cellwise Green formulas and comparing with the global distributional identity yields $\sum_{F=K^+\cap K^-\,\mathrm{interior}}\int_F\phi(v_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+v_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-})=0$. Each normal sum is constant on its facet. If one were nonzero, choose a nonnegative smooth test supported in a small ball around a relative-interior point of that facet, meeting no other facet, and positive on a subpatch; the sum would be a nonzero constant times a positive surface integral, a contradiction. Hence all interior fluxes match.

Suppose the interior fluxes match. For $w\in H^1(D)$, approximate each restriction $w|_K$ in H1 by smooth-neighborhood functions using [F5]. The trace bound [F4] and volume convergence pass cellwise Gauss–Green to each restriction. Interior traces of $w$ agree by [F4], and the normal components of $v$ agree by step 2.1, so interior terms cancel. If $c_F$ denotes the constant outward normal component on a boundary facet $F$, the resulting identity is $\int_D(v\cdot\nabla w+\operatorname{div}v\,w)=\sum_{F\subset\partial D}c_F\int_F\gamma_Fw$. By [F6] this is the weak normal-trace functional; in particular, if every boundary flux is zero then $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$.

Conversely, if $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, its zero trace and the identity in step 4.1 give $\sum_{F\subset\partial D}c_F\int_F\gamma_Fw=0$ for every $w\in H^1(D)$. For any selected boundary facet, choose a smooth function on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in a small ball about a relative-interior point of that facet, positive on a subpatch, and meeting no other boundary facet; its restriction lies in $H^1(D)$. The sum then reduces to the selected $c_F$ times a positive surface integral, so $c_F=0$. Thus every boundary facet flux vanishes.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain, $d\in\{2,3\}$, and set $V:=H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ and $Q:=L^2_0(D)$ with the real graph and integral inner products from [[def-na-hdiv-space]] and [[lem-na-l2-zero-mean-hilbert]]. A permeability tensor $K(x)$ is a measurable real symmetric $d\times d$ matrix field for which there are constants $0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_{\max}<\infty$ satisfying
$$\kappa_{\min}|\xi|^2\le \xi\cdot K(x)\xi\le\kappa_{\max}|\xi|^2$$
for almost every $x\in D$ and every $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$. It is positive definite almost everywhere, so $K^{-1}$ is measurable and has eigenvalues between $\kappa_{\max}^{-1}$ and $\kappa_{\min}^{-1}$. Define
$$a(u,v):=\int_DK^{-1}u\cdot v,\qquad b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v,$$
and the weighted flux norm $\|v\|_{K^{-1}}:=a(v,v)^{1/2}$. For data $F\in V'$ and $f\in Q$, the no-flow mixed Darcy problem is to find $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ such that
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v)\quad(v\in V),\qquad b(u,q)=-\int_D f q\quad(q\in Q).$$
The pressure space's zero-mean constraint fixes the additive constant (Neumann) gauge; $u\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ encodes zero weak normal flux on the full boundary. In the standard source-only Darcy problem used for hybridization, $F=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded, connected polyhedral Lipschitz domain. A matching affine simplicial mesh and its shape regularity have the exact meaning of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]; additionally, call the mesh facet-connected when its dual graph (one vertex per cell and one edge per shared $(d-1)$-facet) is connected. Write $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$.

For $k\ge0$, $\mathbb P_k(K)$ is the real scalar polynomial space of total degree at most $k$, and $\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k$ is the real homogeneous scalar polynomial space of degree exactly $k$ (for $k=0$, the constants). Define
$$\operatorname{RT}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)+x\widetilde{\mathbb P}_k(K),\qquad \operatorname{BDM}_k(K)=\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb R^d)\quad(k\ge1).$$
For either local family $X_k$, its global H(div)-conforming space is
$$X_k(\mathcal T_h)=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};D):v|_K\in X_k(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T_h\}.
$$
The zero-normal RT0 flux space and mean-zero P0 pressure space are
$$V_h:=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D),\qquad Q_h:=\{q\in L^2(D):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K,\ \int_Dq=0\}.$$
For each mesh facet $F$, fix one unit normal $n_F$; on a cell boundary use the outward unit normal $n_K$, which equals either $n_F$ or $-n_F$. The notation $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ means cellwise constants. No existence of a mesh for every $D$ is asserted by this definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open. If $v\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, then $\operatorname{div}v\in L^1(D)$ and
$$\int_D\operatorname{div}v\,dx=0.$$

For a finite conforming simplicial mesh of bounded $D$, define $P_0:L^2(D)\to\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ cellwise by
$$ (P_0g)|_K=|K|^{-1}\int_Kg. $$
Then $P_0$ is linear, equals the identity on piecewise constants, is the $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto that space, satisfies $\|P_0g\|_2\le\|g\|_2$, and preserves the integral $\int_DP_0g=\int_Dg$.

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh conventions of [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. On each $d$-simplex $K$, $\operatorname{RT}_0(K)=\{a+cx:a\in\mathbb R^d,c\in\mathbb R\}$ has dimension $d+1$, and the $d+1$ integrated outward facet-normal fluxes determine its element uniquely. A piecewise RT0 field belongs to $H(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its oriented integrated fluxes match across every shared facet; such a field belongs to $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its normal component (equivalently its integrated outward flux) also vanishes on every boundary facet.

$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$

$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by

the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

derivations.claim: Let $a_F$ be the vertex opposite facet $F$ in $K$ and define $\phi_{K,F}(x)=(x-a_F)/(d|K|)$. On $F$, $(x-a_F)\cdot n_K$ is the altitude $H_F$, so $\int_F\phi_{K,F}\cdot n_K=H_F|F|/(d|K|)=1$ by the simplex pyramid identity $d|K|=H_F|F|$. On any other facet, $a_F$ and $x$ lie in its hyperplane, hence $\phi_{K,F}\cdot n_K=0$. Thus $I_Kv=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}m_{K,F}(v)\phi_{K,F}$, where $m_{K,F}$ is the outward moment. By [F2], [F7], and Cauchy–Schwarz, $|m_{K,F}(v)|\le C(h_K^{(d-2)/2}\|v\|_K+h_K^{d/2}\|\nabla v\|_K)$. Also [F3] gives $\|\phi_{K,F}\|_K\le C h_K|K|^{-1/2}\le C h_K^{1-d/2}$. Multiplying and summing the fixed $d+1$ terms proves $\|I_Kv\|_K\le C(\|v\|_K+h_K\|\nabla v\|_K)$. Squaring and summing cells yields the global stability estimate since $h_K\le h$.

The divergence of $I_Kv\in\operatorname{RT}_0(K)$ is constant. For smooth-neighborhood approximants to $v|_K$ from [F5], Gauss–Green [F4] says the sum of their outward facet moments equals the integral of their divergence. The trace bound [F2] and H1 convergence let both sides pass to the limit, so $\int_K\operatorname{div}I_Kv=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}m_{K,F}(v)=\int_K\operatorname{div}v$. Dividing by $|K|$ gives the stated cell average.

If $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, choose compactly supported smooth vector fields converging to it in H1 by [F5]. Their boundary facet moments are zero; the trace bound [F2] passes this zero moment to $v$. Hence $I_hv$ has zero boundary facet flux, and [F1] gives membership in $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$; [F6] then gives $I_hv\in V_h$.

derivations.claim: Start with a hybrid solution. Its jump constraints and zero boundary flux, together with [F2], make $u_h$ a member of $V_h$. Summing the cell balances against any cellwise constant mean-zero $q_h$ gives the discrete second mixed equation.

Conversely let $(u_h,p_h)$ be the unique conforming solution. Its cell balances hold by [F4]. Let $W_h$ be the broken flux space and define the jump map $J:W_h\to\mathbb R^{\mathcal F_h^i}$ by $J_F(v)=\int_F(v_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+v_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-})$. Its kernel consists of fields with matching interior fluxes, hence lies in $V_h$ by [F2]. Define $\ell(v)=\sum_K[a_K(u_h,v_K)-\int_Kp_h\operatorname{div}v_K]$. The conforming first equation gives $\ell=0$ on $\ker J$.

Suppose there are at least two cells. Every cell is incident to an interior facet because the dual graph is connected and has more than one vertex. The local space $W_K$ therefore contains a basis flux with nonzero total outward flux, so $D_K:W_K\to\mathbb R$, $D_Kv=\int_K\operatorname{div}v$, is onto. The homogeneous local saddle block has equations $a_K(u,v)-pD_Kv=0$ for all $v\in W_K$ and $D_Ku=0$. Taking $v=u$ gives $a_K(u,u)=0$, so [F6] gives $u=0$; then surjectivity of $D_K$ forces $p=0$. The square finite-dimensional block is injective and hence invertible.

Let $c=|D|^{-1}\sum_K|K|p_K$ and set $\bar p_K=p_K-c$. Then $\bar p\in Q_h$. Sum the local first equations against a conforming test $v_h\in V_h$. The facet-multiplier terms cancel by normal continuity; the constant pressure term contributes $-c\int_D\operatorname{div}v_h=0$ by [F7]. The remaining equation is $a(u_h,v_h)-\int_D\bar p\operatorname{div}v_h=0$. Thus $(u_h,\bar p)$ is the conforming mixed solution, which is unique by [F3].

The map $J$ is onto: for each interior facet $F$, use [F5] on one adjacent cell with zero flux on its other facets and zero field on all other cells; its image is the coordinate vector for $F$. Since $\ell$ vanishes on $\ker J$, the formula $\mu(Jv):=\ell(v)$ is well-defined and linear on $\mathbb R^{\mathcal F_h^i}$. Write $\mu(y)=\sum_F\mu_Fy_F$ and choose $\lambda_F=-\mu_F$. Then $\ell(v)+\sum_F\lambda_FJ_F(v)=0$ for all broken $v$. Taking tests supported in one cell yields each local hybrid equation; balances were already shown, so $(u_h,p_h,\lambda)$ is hybrid. This proves the correspondence before quotienting the pressure gauge.

Invert the local blocks to express each $(u_K,p_K)$ as an affine function of the multiplier vector $\lambda$, with source-dependent right sides. Substitution into $J_F(u)=0$ gives a linear system solely on the finitely many interior-facet multipliers; this is static condensation. Existence and correspondence follow from steps 1.1–2.2. For its homogeneous nullspace, any multiplier vector yields a homogeneous hybrid solution, hence by step 2.1 a conforming solution with zero source. Uniqueness [F3] forces $u=0$ and $p_K=c$ for one global constant. The local equations then read $\sum_{F\subset\partial K,\ F\mathrm{interior}}(\lambda_F-c)\int_Fv_K\cdot n_K=0$ for all $v_K\in W_K$, since Gauss–Green and the zero physical-boundary flux give $D_Kv_K=\sum_{F\mathrm{interior}}\int_Fv_K\cdot n_K$. Using the independent facet basis [F5] gives $\lambda_F=c$ on every interior facet. Conversely a common constant vector is a null vector by the gauge identity in [F1]. Thus the kernel is exactly the constant gauge.

For one cell there are no interior multipliers. All its facets are physical boundary facets, so zero boundary flux and local unisolvence [F2] force $W_K=\{0\}$; also $Q_h=\{0\}$. Assume Countable Choice for the published Sobolev interfaces cited below. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and use real scalars. $L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$ means the $d$-tuple of real $L^2$ equivalence classes, with norm $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d\|v_j\|_2^2$. The test space $C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R)$ consists of real smooth functions compactly supported in $D$.

For $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d)$, say that $g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)$ is its distributional divergence when
$$
\int_D v\cdot\nabla\phi\,dx=-\int_D g\phi\,dx\qquad\text{for every }\phi\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R).
$$
The $L^2$ class $g$ is unique when it exists. Indeed, if $g_1,g_2$ both satisfy the identity, put $h=g_1-g_2\in L^2(D)$. Every compact $C\subset D$ has finite Lebesgue measure by [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $\int_C|h|\le |C|^{1/2}\|h\|_{L^2(D)}<\infty$. Thus $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Subtracting the two divergence identities gives $\int_Dh\phi=0$ for every real test $\phi$; splitting a complex test into real and imaginary parts gives the same identity for complex tests. Injectivity of the regular-distribution map in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]] therefore yields $h=0$ almost everywhere, hence $g_1=g_2$ as $L^2$ classes. Define
$$
H(\operatorname{div};D):=\{v\in L^2(D;\mathbb R^d):\text{there is }g\in L^2(D;\mathbb R)\text{ with }g=\operatorname{div}v\text{ distributionally}\},
$$
and equip it with the graph norm
$$
\|v\|_{H(\operatorname{div};D)}:=\bigl(\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}.
$$
The Sobolev notation $H^1(D)=W^{1,2}(D)$ and $H^1_0(D)=W^{1,2}_0(D)$ uses the norm and zero-boundary closure conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] and [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]. No pointwise boundary value is part of this definition.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The affine formulas $p_1(x,y)=y$ and $p_2(x,y)=x$ agree on $x=y$ and attain the four stated vertex values, so they define a continuous piecewise-P1 function. Their negative gradients are $q_1=(0,-1)$ and $q_2=(-1,0)$, each with classical divergence zero. To see it cannot be an $L^2$ function, choose a nonnegative smooth $\psi$ supported in the open diagonal with positive line integral and a smooth transverse cutoff $\eta$ with $\eta(0)=1$; set $\phi_\varepsilon(y,t)=\psi(y)\eta(t/\varepsilon)$ in tubular coordinates, extended by zero. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected Lipschitz polyhedral domain, $d\in\{2,3\}$, and set $V:=H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ and $Q:=L^2_0(D)$ with the real graph and integral inner products from [[def-na-hdiv-space]] and [[lem-na-l2-zero-mean-hilbert]]. A permeability tensor $K(x)$ is a measurable real symmetric $d\times d$ matrix field for which there are constants $0<\kappa_{\min}\le\kappa_{\max}<\infty$ satisfying
$$\kappa_{\min}|\xi|^2\le \xi\cdot K(x)\xi\le\kappa_{\max}|\xi|^2$$
for almost every $x\in D$ and every $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$. It is positive definite almost everywhere, so $K^{-1}$ is measurable and has eigenvalues between $\kappa_{\max}^{-1}$ and $\kappa_{\min}^{-1}$. Define
$$a(u,v):=\int_DK^{-1}u\cdot v,\qquad b(v,q):=-\int_Dq\,\operatorname{div}v,$$
and the weighted flux norm $\|v\|_{K^{-1}}:=a(v,v)^{1/2}$. For data $F\in V'$ and $f\in Q$, the no-flow mixed Darcy problem is to find $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ such that
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v)\quad(v\in V),\qquad b(u,q)=-\int_D f q\quad(q\in Q).$$
The pressure space's zero-mean constraint fixes the additive constant (Neumann) gauge; $u\in H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ encodes zero weak normal flux on the full boundary. In the standard source-only Darcy problem used for hybridization, $F=0$.

Assume Countable Choice, the Darcy data in [[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]], and a facet-connected shape-regular mesh. For at least two cells, set $C_R$ as in the stable lift theorem and define
$$\widehat\beta=(1+C_R^2)^{-1/2},\quad M_a=\kappa_{\min}^{-1},\quad M_b=1,\quad\alpha_*=\kappa_{\max}^{-1}.$$
Let $(u,p)$ solve the continuous source-only Darcy problem ($F=0$) and $(u_h,p_h)$ the RT0/P0 Galerkin system. For any $w_h\in V_h,r_h\in Q_h$, put $\delta_u=\|u-w_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}$, $\delta_p=\|p-r_h\|_2$, and
$$R_h=\widehat\beta^{-1}M_b\delta_u,$$
$$U_h=\delta_u+\alpha_*^{-1}\{M_a(\delta_u+R_h)+M_b\delta_p\}+R_h,$$
$$P_h=\delta_p+\widehat\beta^{-1}\{M_a(U_h+\delta_u)+M_b\delta_p\}.$$
Then the discrete pair exists uniquely and
$$\|u-u_h\|_{H(\operatorname{div})}\le U_h,\qquad \|p-p_h\|_2\le P_h,\qquad \|u-u_h\|_{K^{-1}}\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1/2}U_h.$$
For a one-cell mesh $V_h=Q_h=\{0\}$, so the unique discrete pair is $(0,0)$; the nonzero-$Q_h$ error theorem is not invoked. The constants display permeability contrast and do not assert contrast-independent robustness.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Assume the no-flow Darcy data of [[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]] and a facet-connected conforming mesh from [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. Let $\mathcal F_h^i$ be its interior facets. On each cell $K$, let
$$W_K:=\{v\in\operatorname{RT}_0(K):v\cdot n_K=0\text{ on every boundary facet of }D\text{ contained in }\partial K\}.$$
The broken flux space is $W_h:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T_h}W_K$, the cell pressure space is $M_h:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\mathbb R$, and the skeleton multiplier space is $\Lambda_h:=\prod_{F\in\mathcal F_h^i}\mathbb R$. The scalar $\lambda_F$ is constant on facet $F$ and uses the fixed orientation only to label that facet; local equations use the outward normal of each cell.

For the source-only problem $F=0$, a hybrid solution $(u_h,p_h,\lambda_h)\in W_h\times M_h\times\Lambda_h$ for $f\in Q$ satisfies, for every cell $K$, every $v_K\in W_K$, and every interior facet $F=K^+\cap K^-$,
$$\int_KK^{-1}u_K\cdot v_K-\int_Kp_K\operatorname{div}v_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K,\ F\in\mathcal F_h^i}\lambda_F\int_Fv_K\cdot n_K=0,$$
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}u_K=\int_Kf,$$
$$\int_F(u_{K^+}\cdot n_{K^+}+u_{K^-}\cdot n_{K^-})=0.$$
Because each RT0 normal component is constant on a facet, the last equation is pointwise normal-flux matching. With physical-boundary flux zero, the transformation $p_K\mapsto p_K+c$ for all cells and $\lambda_F\mapsto\lambda_F+c$ leaves the hybrid equations unchanged: in the local first equation the change is $-c\int_K\operatorname{div}v_K+c\sum_{F\text{ interior}}\int_Fv_K\cdot n_K=0$ by Gauss–Green and the zero physical-boundary flux; the mass and jump equations do not use pressure or multipliers. This is the common pressure gauge.

Assume Countable Choice and the source-only Darcy system and hybrid equations of [[def-na-hybridized-rt0-darcy-system]] on a facet-connected mesh. The hybrid solutions modulo the common pressure shift $(p,\lambda)\mapsto(p+c,\lambda+c)$ are in one-to-one correspondence with the conforming RT0/P0 Darcy solution. If the mesh has at least two cells, every local flux-pressure saddle block is invertible; eliminating these local variables gives a linear system on the interior-facet multipliers whose nullspace is exactly the one-dimensional constant gauge. For one cell, the conforming flux and mean-zero pressure spaces are zero and the hybrid pressure is entirely gauge.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a nondegenerate affine $d$-simplex and let
$G\in C^1(\overline K;\mathbb R^d)$. If $n_{K,F}$ is the outward unit
normal on each facet $F$, then
$$\int_K\operatorname{div}G\,dx=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_FG\cdot n_{K,F}\,dS.$$
For an orientation-preserving affine map $F_K(\widehat x)=b+A\widehat x$,
the oriented area element transforms as
$$n_{K,F}\,dS=\det(A)A^{-T}\widehat n_{\widehat F}\,d\widehat S.$$

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh conventions of [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. On each $d$-simplex $K$, $\operatorname{RT}_0(K)=\{a+cx:a\in\mathbb R^d,c\in\mathbb R\}$ has dimension $d+1$, and the $d+1$ integrated outward facet-normal fluxes determine its element uniquely. A piecewise RT0 field belongs to $H(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its oriented integrated fluxes match across every shared facet; such a field belongs to $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$ exactly when its normal component (equivalently its integrated outward flux) also vanishes on every boundary facet.

derivations.claim: Each cell has area $1/2$. The field $\theta_1=(x-1,y)$ has zero normal component on $x=1$ and $y=0$, and unit integrated outward flux on the diagonal from $K_1$; $\theta_2=(x,y-1)$ has zero normal component on $x=0$ and $y=1$, and unit integrated outward flux on the diagonal from $K_2$. Their divergences are both $2$, so $\int_{K_i}\operatorname{div}\theta_i=1$ by [F3]. The two zero-boundary conditions and the single free facet degree of freedom make each $\theta_i$ a basis of its local space by [F4]. Direct integration gives $\int_{K_1}|\theta_1|^2=\int_0^1\int_0^x((x-1)^2+y^2)\,dy\,dx=\tfrac16,$ and reflection symmetry gives $\int_{K_2}|\theta_2|^2=1/6$.

Write $u_i=t_i\theta_i$. The cell balances in [F1] give $t_1=\int_{K_1}f=1/2$ and $t_2=\int_{K_2}f=-1/2$. For a local test $v_i=s\theta_i$, its integrated divergence is $s$ and its interior outward flux is $s$. The first hybrid equation is therefore $t_i s/6-p_i s+\lambda s=0$ for every real $s$, equivalently $t_i/6-p_i+\lambda=0$. The jump equation is $t_1+t_2=0$, which the balance values satisfy.

Solving the local equations gives $p_1=1/12+\lambda$ and $p_2=-1/12+\lambda$. Since the cells have equal area, their global mean is $\lambda$; choose the mean-zero gauge $\lambda=0$ to obtain the stated pressures. After local elimination the single skeleton equation is $t_1+t_2=0$, independent of $\lambda$, so its one-dimensional nullspace consists exactly of common constant shifts. This is the constant gauge described in [F2].
